title: Exploring AI-Enabled Test Practice, Affect, and Test Outcomes in Language Assessment
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether repeated access to AI-enabled practice tests is associated with better outcomes in a high-stakes language assessment context. The authors focus on the Duolingo English Test (DET) and ask how the number of practice tests taken relates to official DET scores, test-taker affect such as confidence and preparedness, and whether test takers choose to share their scores for university admissions. The core motivation is that generative AI-based automated item generation (AIG) makes it possible to scale large item banks and produce many distinct practice tests, which may change how learners prepare for high-stakes exams.

The intervention or approach studied is not an experimental treatment but the real-world use of the DET’s free AI-generated, computer-adaptive practice tests. These practice tests are built from AIG-created item pools with human review and are designed to familiarize users with the official exam format, item types, and scoring range. The study is a large-scale observational analysis of 25,969 first-time official DET test takers who completed a short post-test affect survey in September 2023 and had taken zero or more DET practice tests within the prior 60 days.

The population consists of DET test takers using the exam primarily for higher education admissions, including those seeking undergraduate and graduate study; the sample also includes a broader adult test-taking population. The context is an online, high-stakes English proficiency testing environment rather than a classroom. The authors compare official test scores, self-reported affect, and score-sharing behavior across groups defined by number of practice tests taken (0, 1, 2-3, 4-6, 7+).

The main conclusions are that taking 1-3 practice tests was associated with slightly higher official DET scores, more positive affect, and higher likelihood of score sharing, especially among those reporting confidence, preparedness, or having achieved their desired score. However, taking more than 3 practice tests was associated with lower performance on average, which the authors suggest may reflect washback effects, lower underlying proficiency, or use of practice tests for purposes beyond test familiarization. The paper emphasizes that these findings are correlational rather than causal, but argues that AI-supported test practice may be beneficial when used in moderation and raises important questions about best practices for AI-enhanced test readiness in high-stakes assessment.

identified_tools.name: Duolingo
identified_tools.description: Duolingo is a language-learning and assessment platform; in this paper it includes the Duolingo English Test (DET), an AI-driven high-stakes computer-adaptive English proficiency assessment with generative-AI-enabled automated item generation for practice-test item banks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied the DET's AIG-enabled practice tests, examining how the number of practice tests taken within 60 days before a first official DET attempt related to official DET scores, self-reported affect, and score-sharing for university admissions.

findings.finding_summary: In this large observational study, official DET performance varied by number of AIG-enabled practice tests taken (N=25,969). Mean DET scores were 108.5 for 0 practice tests (95% CI [107.8, 109.2]), 112.4 for 1 test ([111.8, 113.0]), 112.3 for 2–3 tests ([111.8, 112.8]), 111.1 for 4–6 tests ([110.5, 111.7]), and 108.6 for 7+ tests ([108.1, 109.1]); the authors report that 1–3 practice tests were associated with higher scores, while 4+ was associated with lower performance.
findings.measure: Official Duolingo English Test overall score by number of practice tests taken

findings.finding_summary: Positive affect toward the official DET increased with more practice-test use: the paper states that higher proportions of test takers reported positive affect (achieved desired score, confidence, motivation, preparedness) as the number of practice tests increased, with the 7+ group consistently having the highest proportion reporting positive affect. Anxiety was similar across practice-test groups, and no significant relationship between anxiety and number of practice tests was found.
findings.measure: Post-test survey of affective perceptions: achieved desired score, confidence, motivation, preparedness, anxiety

findings.finding_summary: Score-sharing for university admissions was more likely among test takers with positive affect, especially among those taking 0–3 practice tests. For example, for the 'Achieved' item, share rates were 41.9% vs 32.2% (0 tests), 43.5% vs 31.9% (1 test), and 43.4% vs 33.6% (2–3 tests) for Agree vs Disagree, with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals reported for these groups; similar patterns held for Confident and Prepared, and for Motivated in the 2–3 test group.
findings.measure: Proportion of test takers who shared DET scores for university admissions by affect and number of practice tests
findings.confidence_interval: Achieved 0 PT Agree [40.3, 43.4] vs Disagree [28.6, 35.7]; 1 PT [42.1, 44.8] vs [29.1, 34.7]; 2–3 PT [42.1, 44.7] vs [30.7, 36.5]. Additional CIs reported in Table 5 for Confident, Motivated, Prepared, and Anxious.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a large-scale empirical observational study, but the authors explicitly note that findings are not causal. There is no random assignment or quasi-experimental design, so the evidence is correlational.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful directional differences in scores, affect, and score-sharing, but no standardized effect sizes are provided and the design is observational. Impact therefore appears suggestive but unclear in magnitude.
